specPoints.text: understand why an increase in temperature results in an increase in the average speed of gas molecules
know that the Kelvin temperature of a gas is proportional to the average kinetic energy of its molecules

primer.text: A thermometer is a speedometer for molecules. Warm the gas and the average molecular speed rises; cool it and the swarm slows. Better still, the kelvin temperature is exactly proportional to the average kinetic energy — the proportionality that makes every gas law work.

lessons.title: Temperature and molecular speed
lessons.opening: Heat a sealed gas and the molecules do not drift in a preferred direction — they simply move faster in every direction. The speed distribution shifts upward: more molecules at every higher speed, same chaos, hotter gas.
keyPoints: Gas molecules move randomly with a range of speeds at any temperature.
Increasing the temperature increases the average speed of the molecules.
Heating transfers energy into the molecules' kinetic store.
The direction of molecular motion stays random as the speeds rise.
Cooling the gas lowers the average molecular speed.

low.restatement: Warm the gas, and its molecules zip about faster; chill it, and they slow. The directions stay random — only the pace changes with temperature.
low.analogy: A dance floor where the DJ raises the tempo: everyone keeps dancing every which way, but the whole crowd moves quicker.
low.examPointer: Say 'average speed increases' — individual molecules still vary, and the randomness of direction never becomes ordered flow.

medium.restatement: The molecules hold a spread of speeds described by a distribution, not a single value. Supplied energy raises the whole distribution: the mean speed grows, the spread widens, but the velocity vectors remain isotropic, so no bulk flow appears. The temperature rise is precisely the growth of mean translational kinetic energy.
medium.analogy: A crowded motorway at rush hour versus midnight: every car still picks its own lane and direction, but the average pace on the network rises with the 'temperature' of the traffic.
medium.examPointer: When explaining, connect the energy chain explicitly: heating → energy into molecular kinetic store → higher mean speed → (at fixed volume) harder, more frequent wall impacts.

check.stem: What happens to the average speed of gas molecules when the gas is heated?

options.text: it increases
options.explanation: Heating raises the mean molecular speed.

options.text: it decreases
options.explanation: Cooling, not heating, slows the swarm.

options.text: it stays the same
options.explanation: Speed tracks the energy supplied.

options.text: it becomes zero as they align
options.explanation: Heating never orders the directions.

check.stem: When a gas is heated in a sealed box, what happens to the directions of molecular motion?

options.text: they stay random in all directions
options.explanation: Heating changes speeds, not the isotropy of directions.

options.text: they all align with the heating element
options.explanation: Collisions re-randomise directions instantly.

options.text: they rotate around the box
options.explanation: No bulk rotation appears in a sealed box.

options.text: they point downwards under gravity
options.explanation: Random motion swamps gravity at molecular scale.

check.stem: Where does the extra molecular speed come from when a gas is heated?

options.text: the supplied energy transfers into the molecules' kinetic store
options.explanation: Heating raises the mean translational kinetic energy.

options.text: the molecules multiply in number
options.explanation: The molecule count is fixed in a sealed system.

options.text: the molecules shrink and so travel faster
options.explanation: Size changes nothing; energy does.

options.text: the box pushes them faster
options.explanation: The walls receive collisions; they do not motor the molecules.

check.stem: A gas cools from 400 K to 200 K at constant volume. What happens to the wall collisions?

options.text: molecules hit the walls more slowly and less often, so pressure falls
options.explanation: Slower swarm means weaker, rarer impacts.

options.text: molecules hit the walls harder, so pressure rises
options.explanation: Cooling slows the swarm; pressure falls.

options.text: collisions stop entirely at 200 K
options.explanation: 200 K is far above absolute zero; motion continues.

options.text: collisions are unchanged because volume is fixed
options.explanation: Speed changes with temperature regardless of volume.

check.stem: Why does a balloon of air left in the sun feel firmer as its temperature rises?

options.text: faster molecules strike the rubber harder and more often, raising internal pressure
options.explanation: Speed rise feeds directly into wall bombardment.

options.text: the sun adds molecules to the balloon
options.explanation: The molecule count is sealed inside.

options.text: the rubber contracts in heat, squeezing the air
options.explanation: Rubber expands slightly in heat; the pressure story suffices.

options.text: the molecules align and push in one direction
options.explanation: Directions stay random; pressure rises through totals.

check.stem: State what happens to the average speed of gas molecules as temperature increases.
check.modelAnswer: The average speed of the molecules increases as the temperature rises.

check.stem: State what happens to the direction of molecular motion while a gas is heated.
check.modelAnswer: The directions remain random in all directions — heating changes the speeds, not the pattern of directions.

check.stem: Explain why heating a gas does not cause all its molecules to move at one identical new speed.
check.modelAnswer: Collisions constantly redistribute energy between molecules — one gains in a collision exactly what another loses. The result is a spread of speeds around a rising mean, not a single value. Heating lifts the whole distribution of speeds; it does not synchronise the molecules.

check.stem: A sealed aerosol can warns against incineration. Using molecular speed, explain the danger.
check.modelAnswer: In a fire the can's temperature rises sharply, so the average molecular speed of the propellant gas increases greatly. The faster swarm strikes the can's walls harder and far more often, raising the internal pressure beyond what the can can withstand, so it may explode.

lessons.title: Kelvin temperature and average kinetic energy
lessons.opening: The precise statement behind 'hotter means faster' is a proportionality: kelvin temperature and the mean kinetic energy of the molecules rise in lockstep. Double the kelvin temperature and the mean molecular energy doubles — the ladder every gas law climbs.
keyPoints: Kelvin temperature scales directly with the mean kinetic energy carried by the molecules.
At 0 K the average kinetic energy of the molecules is at its minimum.
Doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the average molecular kinetic energy.
The proportionality is why kelvin must be used in gas-law equations.
Average kinetic energy refers to the mean over all molecules, not to any single molecule.

low.restatement: Kelvin temperature and the molecules' average kinetic energy rise and fall together: double one and you double the other. At absolute zero that energy bottoms out.
low.analogy: A fuel gauge wired to the tank: the needle (temperature) and the fuel (energy) are locked together by design.
low.examPointer: Use the word 'proportional', not 'equal' — temperature is not the energy itself; it is proportional to it.

medium.restatement: The proportionality T ∝ mean translational KE is the kinetic definition of temperature, and it anchors why 0 K is unreachable-but-defined: it is the energy origin. Because the relation is linear through the true zero, temperature ratios in kelvin are energy ratios, which is exactly the property the pressure law and Charles-type arguments require.
medium.analogy: Staircases rising from the same ground floor: only from the common ground can 'twice as high' mean anything — and 0 K is that ground for molecular energy.
medium.examPointer: In evaporation questions, the survival chain is: the most energetic molecules leave, the average KE of the remainder falls, and since kelvin temperature is proportional to that average, the temperature falls. Quote all three links.

check.stem: Kelvin temperature is proportional to which molecular quantity?

options.text: the average kinetic energy of the molecules
options.explanation: T ∝ mean KE is the kinetic definition.

options.text: the average mass of the molecules
options.explanation: Mass is fixed per gas; temperature tracks energy.

options.text: the number of molecules
options.explanation: Count is independent of temperature.

options.text: the average size of the molecules
options.explanation: Size never enters the temperature definition.

check.stem: A gas's kelvin temperature doubles. What happens to the average molecular kinetic energy?

options.text: it doubles
options.explanation: Proportionality is linear in kelvin.

options.text: it quadruples
options.explanation: Quadrupling would need a squared relation, which this is not.

options.text: it halves
options.explanation: Heating raises the energy.

options.text: it stays constant
options.explanation: Energy tracks temperature.

check.stem: A liquid evaporates, its most energetic molecules escaping. What happens to the temperature of what remains, and why?

options.text: it falls, because the average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules falls
options.explanation: Selective loss drags the mean down, and temperature tracks the mean.

options.text: it rises, because evaporation adds energy
options.explanation: Evaporation removes the energetic tail of the distribution.

options.text: it stays the same because the molecule count fell too
options.explanation: Count is irrelevant; the average energy fell.

options.text: it becomes undefined
options.explanation: The remaining molecules still define a temperature.

check.stem: Why must kelvin — not Celsius — be used when reasoning about energy ratios in a gas?

options.text: kelvin's zero coincides with zero molecular kinetic energy, so ratios are energy ratios
options.explanation: Only from the true zero do ratios carry meaning.

options.text: Celsius values are too small to compute with
options.explanation: Size is irrelevant; the origin is the issue.

options.text: Celsius thermometers are less accurate
options.explanation: Accuracy is not the problem; the reference point is.

options.text: kelvin has smaller units
options.explanation: The units are identical in size.

check.stem: Two samples of the same gas are at 300 K and 600 K. Compare their mean molecular speeds.

options.text: the hotter sample's molecules have twice the average kinetic energy, so a higher average speed
options.explanation: Energy doubles with kelvin; speed rises accordingly.

options.text: the hotter sample's average speed is exactly half
options.explanation: Speed rises with temperature, it does not halve.

options.text: both samples have equal average speeds
options.explanation: Different temperatures mean different mean energies.

options.text: the hotter sample's molecules have half the kinetic energy
options.explanation: Higher temperature is higher energy.

check.stem: State the proportionality between Kelvin temperature and molecular energy.
check.modelAnswer: Kelvin temperature scales in proportion with the mean kinetic energy of the gas's molecules.

check.stem: State what happens to the average kinetic energy of a gas's molecules between 0 K and any higher temperature.
check.modelAnswer: It rises from its minimum at 0 K in direct proportion to the kelvin temperature.

check.stem: Explain why the temperature of the air inside a pumped bicycle tyre can rise while the pump is worked quickly.
check.modelAnswer: Rapid compression does work on the air, transferring energy into the molecules' kinetic store. The average kinetic energy of the molecules rises, and since kelvin temperature is proportional to that average, the air's temperature rises — the fast-moving swarm is hotter before any heat even conducts to the frame.

check.stem: A science fiction story claims a gas was chilled to −300 °C. Show with a conversion that this is unphysical.
check.modelAnswer: −300 °C would be −300 + 273 = −27 K on the kelvin scale. Negative kelvin is below absolute zero, where average molecular kinetic energy would be negative — impossible, so the story violates the kinetic model.

glossary.definition: The mean translational kinetic energy of a gas's molecules, proportional to kelvin temperature.
The average speed of the molecules, which rises with temperature and falls on cooling.
The spread of molecular speeds around the mean at any temperature.

workedExample.prompt: When a liquid evaporates, molecules escape from the surface of the liquid. What happens to the temperature of the liquid and the average kinetic energy of the molecules within it? A — both increase; B — both decrease; C — both stay the same; D — temperature decreases while average kinetic energy increases.
steps: Evaporation is selective: the most energetic molecules are the ones that leave the surface first.
With the energetic tail gone, the average kinetic energy per molecule of those remaining must decrease.
Options A and D fail because the average energy falls rather than rises or stays fixed.
Because kelvin temperature tracks the mean kinetic energy per molecule, the temperature falls too.
workedExample.finalAnswer: B — both the temperature of the liquid and the average kinetic energy of its remaining molecules decrease.
